new.readme: Your agents, talking to your teammates' agents. End-to-end encrypted, peer to peer. One small daemon per computer. Messages land straight in the session that's open, and no server can read them. Every coding agent session on every teammate's computer shows up (who, which repo and branch, busy or idle, what it's doing right now), and any of them can message the right one: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Copilot CLI, Grok CLI, opencode, pi, DeepSeek Harness and Reason.

threats.title: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys compromised
threats.headline: Recoverable eMudhra intermediate CA keys let attackers impersonate any site to clients with outdated trust stores
threats.summary: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates were incorrectly generated and can be recovered from the certificates. Six are TLS intermediates trusted by the Chrome, Mozilla, Microsoft and Apple root programs, and two are codesigning intermediates trusted by Microsoft. An attacker with any of the keys could impersonate any website or service to clients that still trust them, notably clients outside browsers that do not enforce Certificate Transparency.
actions: Update Python certifi to 2026.10.19 or later
Update Rust rustls-webpki to 0.103.16 or later
Update curl CA bundle to 2026-10-20 or later
Update Homebrew ca-certificates to 2026-09-25_1 or later
Update Claude Code to 2.1.303 or later
Update Docker Desktop to 4.96.2 or later
Update browsers and operating systems promptly.

action_quotes.action: Update browsers and operating systems promptly.
action_quotes.quote: Users should update their browsers and operating systems to the latest versions as soon as possible.

who: TLS clients outside browsers that do not enforce Certificate Transparency
tools using bundled trust stores such as certifi, pip, uv, Node.js and Go
threats.quote: An attacker with the private key of any of the compromised intermediate CAs could impersonate any website or service.

threats.title: uv bundled CA store trusts compromised emSign root
threats.headline: uv's vendored root bundle trusts an emSign root whose intermediate keys are compromised, enabling MITM
threats.summary: uv verifies TLS against a vendored copy of the webpki-root-certs bundle, which in affected versions includes the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 root. Eight eMudhra intermediates chaining to that root have compromised private keys. An attacker with one of the keys can issue certificates that uv accepts for any hostname and use them for MITM attacks.
threats.quote: An attacker with one of the compromised keys can issue certificates that uv accepts for any hostname, and can be used to issue certificates to enable MITM attacks.

threats.title: certifi bundles emSign root with compromised intermediates
threats.headline: certifi CA bundle trusts emSign root tied to compromised intermediate keys, exposing requests, urllib3 and pip
threats.summary: An attacker with a key can issue valid-looking certificates for any hostname.
actions: Rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

action_quotes.action: Rebuild container images that vendor certifi.
action_quotes.quote: Upgrade to 2026.10.19 or later, and rebuild container images that vendor certifi.

who: Python apps using requests, urllib3 or pip
threats.quote: If the attacker is also on-path, they can intercept or modify TLS traffic from clients that trust the certifi bundle.

threats.title: rustls-webpki may accept compromised emSign intermediates

threats.summary: The private keys for these intermediates are now well known. Fixed versions reject paths containing these public keys.
threats.quote: The private keys corresponding to these intermediates are now well known.

items.connection: Flint provides a laptop-class open coding model, Graphify gives it local repo context with explained edges, and OpenCode supplies the open agent loop, so the whole stack runs with no network calls.
items.context: many regulated firms cannot send code to third-party APIs
chain: A coding model built for laptops arrives as open weights, alongside a local, deterministic code knowledge graph.
OpenCode can drive the local model while Graphify answers repo questions without a vector store or cloud service.
Teams barred from cloud coding tools get an agent they can run inside a secure enclave and audit edge by edge.
Security reviewers can approve the setup faster because every context lookup is explainable, which shortens procurement for cleared work.
items.who: Engineers at defense, government and critical-infrastructure contractors benefit; their IT security and engineering budgets pay for laptops and integration.
items.variable: time from ticket to first reviewed patch on restricted repos
items.versus: Today these teams get no coding agent at all, and closed products cannot pass an air-gap requirement.
items.smallest_test: On one disconnected laptop, run OpenCode with Flint plus a Graphify index of an internal repo on 20 real tickets; success if at least 8 yield patches a senior engineer accepts with minor edits.
items.disconfirm: Flint's license forbids this use, or fewer than 4 of 20 tickets produce acceptable patches on laptop hardware.

items.title: Open source maintainers can triage agent-found vulnerabilities locally before disclosure deadlines
items.connection: Patch the Planet signals a coming flood of agent-found bugs, Graphify maps the blast radius of each one with explained edges, and Sage-A1.5 runs the triage agent cheaply on modest hardware without sharing undisclosed bugs.
items.context: undisclosed vulnerability details should not leave the maintainer's control
chain: OpenAI starts coordinating disclosure because agents may find bugs faster than maintainers can fix them.
Report volume rises, and the scarce resource becomes maintainer hours spent judging which reports matter.
A local graph of code, configs and schemas lets a small agentic model trace which entry points reach the flawed function and explain why.
Foundations can offer maintainers a ranked, explained queue, so critical fixes ship first and coordination programs see fewer missed deadlines.
items.who: Volunteer maintainers and open source foundations benefit; foundations, security sponsors and companies depending on the projects would fund it.
items.variable: median days from report to triage decision
items.versus: Doing nothing leaves maintainers reading reports in arrival order, and sending unpatched bug details to a hosted tool adds leak risk.
items.smallest_test: Replay 30 past security reports on one project through Sage-A1.5 plus Graphify; success if its top-10 ranking contains at least 7 of the reports maintainers actually rated high or critical.
items.disconfirm: Graphify reachability traces are wrong on more than a third of reports, or the agent's ranking matches maintainer severity no better than chance.

items.context: retouching costs scale per image; commercial use depends on each model's license
chain: Two editing-focused image models are now available within a week of each other.
A Comfy workflow lets a studio feed the same product photos through both and compare results blind.
The studio picks the winner per task, such as background swaps versus color variants, instead of betting on one model.
Studios can quote catalog refreshes at a lower per-image price, which pressures outsourced retouching shops.
items.who: In-house e-commerce photo teams and small creative agencies benefit; retail marketing budgets pay.
items.versus: Doing nothing keeps manual retouching costs, and committing to one closed editing product locks in pricing before quality is known.
items.smallest_test: Edit 100 product photos with each model for three common tasks and have two retouchers rate them blind; success if one model meets client-ready quality on at least 70 percent of images in a task.
items.disconfirm: Licenses for both models block commercial use, or neither reaches client-ready quality on more than 40 percent of images.
